screens.title: Testing & Quality Assurance in Unity
screens.subtitle: Build confidence with automated tests, playtesting, and disciplined bug workflows

narration.text: Testing and quality assurance are the practices that keep a game playable, stable, and enjoyable. In a project, tests catch regressions early, reduce firefighting, and help teams change code without fear. You will learn how to use the Unity Test Runner, why we separate Edit Mode and Play Mode tests, and where playtesting and human feedback fit into a balanced QA strategy. We’ll walk through concrete unit test examples for gameplay logic, a Play Mode integration test for movement, and a hands-on inventory testing activity that you can implement immediately. Along the way I’ll point out common mistakes, like tests that are too broad or neglecting playtesting. By the end of this chapter you’ll be able to write focused tests that verify single behaviors, design integration checks that cover interactions between systems, and run targeted playtests to capture user-facing issues. Think of tests as documentation that proves assumptions and gives you the freedom to refactor. What small class in your game could you protect with a first unit test?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Combine automated unit and integration tests with structured playtesting and bug workflows to preserve code quality and player experience.

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will understand why testing and QA are essential in game development, and you will be able to create focused unit tests that verify single behaviors. You will also be able to write integration or Play Mode tests that validate interactions between systems such as movement, combat, and UI. In addition, you will learn how to plan and run effective playtests to capture usability and design issues that automated tests cannot find. Finally, you will be introduced to bug reporting and regression testing strategies so fixes remain stable over time. Each objective is rooted in practical examples: we show PlayerStats unit tests, a Play Mode movement integration test, and an Inventory unit-testing activity so you can apply these skills directly. These abilities reduce regressions, speed debugging, and improve player experience because they let you change code with confidence. Think about one gameplay class you touch frequently—after these lessons you should be able to write at least one unit test for a key method in that class and explain when an integration or playtest is required.

screens.title: Why Testing and QA Matter
screens.subtitle: The role of testing in delivering a stable player experience

narration.text: Testing and quality assurance are continuous activities that protect your game from regressions and poor player experiences. At its core QA is a process: identify potential failure modes, verify behavior, and prevent regressions. For a developer this means writing tests that prove assumptions about code, and for designers or producers it means organizing playtests and triaging issues. A common misconception is that automated tests replace human playtesting—automated checks verify deterministic code behavior, but they cannot judge whether a mechanic is fun or confusing. For example, a unit test can confirm a PlayerStats class clamps health to zero, but only playtesting reveals whether the player finds health loss fair or frustrating. Practically, a layered approach works best: unit tests for isolated logic, integration tests for interactions, and playtests for user-facing experience. Start small: protect the smallest, most frequently changed classes first. The takeaway is that testing buys you confidence to refactor, reduces time spent chasing regressions, and captures both technical and design problems when combined with structured playtesting. Which tiny class will you protect first? Why Testing and QA Matter means qa combines automated tests and human playtesting to ensure technical correctness and user-facing quality.. In practical terms, the role of testing in delivering a stable player experience. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: QA combines automated tests and human playtesting to ensure technical correctness and user-facing quality.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Why QA Matters
Definition & value

QA is the set of practices that verify a product meets quality standards. In games, QA reduces user-facing bugs, preserves reputation, and lowers long-term maintenance cost.

Key benefit
Confidence when refactoring and faster iteration cycles.
Misconception
Automated tests don't replace playtesting; they complement it by ensuring technical correctness.
Concrete example
PlayerStats
Unit tests verify TakeDamage, Heal, and IsDead. This prevents simple bugs like health going negative after refactors.
Playtest scenario
Observe a player struggling with a level. Automated tests may not reveal frustration; structured playtests will, guiding design fixes.
Key Takeaway

Combine unit, integration, and playtesting to cover technical correctness and player experience; tests give you safe change windows.

Try this

Pick one class you change often and add a single unit test that would fail if a key assumption breaks.

screens.title: Unity Test Runner — Edit Mode vs Play Mode
screens.subtitle: When to use each test type and how they differ

narration.text: The Unity Test Runner provides two primary execution contexts: Edit Mode tests and Play Mode tests. Edit Mode tests run inside the Editor without playing the scene and are ideal for quick, deterministic checks of pure C# logic. These tests are fast and should be your first line of defense for classes that do not rely on MonoBehaviour lifecycle, scene objects, or physics. Play Mode tests run while the Editor simulates play and are necessary for any test that touches GameObjects, physics, components, or frame-based behavior. For instance, a PlayerStats class that stores integers is well suited for an Edit Mode test, whereas verifying that Rigidbody-based movement changes position over several frames requires a Play Mode test. A common mistake is putting heavy runtime tests in Edit Mode or conversely overusing Play Mode for trivial logic—this makes the test suite slow and brittle. Architect your tests so Edit Mode covers pure logic and Play Mode covers integrations and runtime interactions. Keep Play Mode tests focused and use small waits or frame yields rather than long sleeps to keep tests fast. Which behavior in your project clearly needs Play Mode verification?

keyIdea.title: Test contexts
keyIdea.text: Use Edit Mode for pure logic and Play Mode for runtime interactions; balance speed and coverage by choosing the right context.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Edit vs Play Mode
Contexts
Edit Mode Tests
Fast, run without play; ideal for pure C# classes and deterministic asserts.
Play Mode Tests
Run while the Editor plays; necessary for GameObjects, physics, coroutines, and frame-based checks.
Best practice
Keep Edit Mode broad coverage; reserve Play Mode for interaction tests to keep CI fast.
Concrete scenario
PlayerStats

Test TakeDamage and Heal in Edit Mode because they operate on values and have no GameObject dependencies.

PlayerMovement

Verify forward movement in Play Mode by instantiating a GameObject with a Rigidbody and advancing frames; this checks physics and component interaction.

Common mistake
Placing heavy integration checks in Edit Mode or writing brittle Play Mode tests that rely on long delays.
Pro tip
Mock or separate pure logic so you can test it in Edit Mode and keep Play Mode focused on integration points.
Check
If a test needs a scene, physics, or component updates, use Play Mode; otherwise prefer Edit Mode.

screens.title: Writing Focused Unit Tests
screens.subtitle: Principles for testing single concerns and test hygiene

narration.text: A good unit test isolates one concern, runs deterministically, and asserts a single behavior or outcome. Begin by arranging known state, performing a single action, and asserting expected results. For example, when testing a PlayerStats TakeDamage method: create a PlayerStats instance with a known max health, call TakeDamage with a specific value, and assert the resulting Health matches the expectation. Avoid tests that depend on unrelated systems or random values. Use clear names that document intent, and keep test setup minimal by using helper methods or per-test setup hooks. Another important practice is to test edge cases: negative inputs, over-heal, or damage larger than current health. Tests should be independent so reordering them or running one alone still produces the same result. A common pitfall is writing tests that mirror implementation details instead of behavior; tests tied too closely to internal structure break when you refactor even if behavior is unchanged. Instead, assert public behavior and invariants. Finally, make failing tests easy to debug with meaningful assert messages. Which method in your codebase would benefit most from a focused assert first?

keyIdea.title: Unit test hygiene
keyIdea.text: Arrange, act, assert; test one behavior; prefer public-behavior assertions over implementation details.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Unit Tests
Arrange • Act • Assert
  1. Arrange: Create objects with deterministic state.
  2. Act: Call a single method or perform one action.
  3. Assert: Verify the expected public behavior or invariant.
Edge cases
Always test negative inputs, bounds, and extremes to prevent regressions from surprising values.
Example test (visual)
// Visual pseudo-code of test intent // Setup PlayerStats with 100 max health // Call TakeDamage(20) // Expect Health == 80
Misconception
Tests are not snapshots of implementation. Prefer checking observable behavior, not private fields or internal flow.
Pro tip
Use a test setup method to create repeatable state and helper factories to keep tests concise.
Key Takeaway
Focus tests on behavior; keep them fast and independent so they can run often.

screens.title: PlayerStats Unit Test Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Interpreting tests that protect health logic

narration.text: Let's walk through a set of unit tests for a PlayerStats class to see how tests document expectations and prevent regressions. The tests verify that a player starts at maximum health, that taking damage reduces health appropriately, that health never goes below zero, that healing increases health but never above max, and that negative input values have no harmful side effects. Each test creates a fresh PlayerStats instance so tests are independent. Assertions check final Health values and helper methods like IsDead. For a damage modifier scenario, a test sets the modifier and verifies the multiplied damage effect. When a failing test appears, the failure message should make it clear which behavior broke and why, guiding a quick fix. A typical mistake is to assert intermediate state rather than final behavior; tests that depend on the internal flow can fail during refactors even when behavior is unchanged. By contrast, these unit tests assert clear external outcomes, so refactors that preserve behavior keep tests green. Try adding a test that asserts Heal with a negative amount leaves health unchanged; it protects against an accidental sign inversion. What failure message would help you fix that bug fastest?

keyIdea.title: Example walkthrough
keyIdea.text: Unit tests for PlayerStats make explicit guarantees about starting state, damage, healing, modifiers, and edge cases.

Key Takeaway

screens.title: Play Mode Integration Testing
screens.subtitle: Simulating runtime interactions and frame-based checks

narration.text: Integration tests in Play Mode let you validate interactions across systems: movement, physics, animations, UI updates, and more. A typical Play Mode test instantiates the required GameObjects or prefabs, sets known initial state, triggers an action or simulates input, waits for a small number of frames or yields for a short duration, and then asserts resulting state such as position changes, health updates, or UI visibility. For example, a simple movement integration test creates a player GameObject with a Rigidbody and movement component, records its initial position, calls a movement method or simulates input, yields a few frames, and then asserts that the Z position increased. Avoid long time waits in tests; use small yields and targeted checks to keep tests fast. Integration tests should clean up created GameObjects to avoid side effects. A common pitfall is relying on scene setup that differs between developer machines; instead instantiate required objects in the test so it is deterministic. The final takeaway is to use Play Mode tests to capture multi-system behavior that Edit Mode cannot, while keeping execution fast and isolated so your CI remains responsive.

keyIdea.title: Integration pattern
keyIdea.text: Instantiate necessary runtime objects, perform actions, yield a small number of frames, and assert the integrated behavior deterministically.

Integration steps
Arrange
→
Act
→
Yield & Assert
Arrange required GameObjects and components in the test, act by invoking methods or simulating input, yield a few frames, then assert the expected outcome such as a position change or an animation state.
Concrete example
PlayerMovesForward
Instantiate a cube with Rigidbody and PlayerMovement, set speed, call Move(forward), yield for a short time, assert Z increased.
Cleanup
Destroy created objects at test end to avoid interfering with other tests.
Misconception
Long waits in tests are acceptable — they make suites slow and fragile across machines.
Pro tip
Yield small frame counts and verify specific state changes to keep Play Mode tests fast on CI.
Key Takeaway
Use Play Mode tests for multi-system interactions, but instantiate and cleanup explicitly so tests are deterministic.

screens.title: Unit Testing vs Integration Testing vs Playtesting
screens.subtitle: What each method finds and where it fits in your workflow

narration.text: Unit tests, integration tests, and playtesting each target different failure modes. Unit tests verify single functions or classes in isolation; they catch logic errors and guard simple invariants. Integration tests combine multiple components and find issues that appear when systems interact, such as incorrect data flow between combat and UI. Playtesting is human-centered: it reveals usability problems, confusing mechanics, and performance issues that automated tests cannot judge. A balanced workflow uses all three: write unit tests for stable, frequently changed code; add integration tests around critical flows; and run structured playtests to evaluate design. One common mistake is to rely solely on automated tests; they miss subjective problems and emergent bugs caused by complex player behavior. Conversely, an exclusively manual process leaves code brittle and makes refactors risky. Practical scheduling helps: run unit tests in pre-commit or CI, run targeted integration tests on pull requests, and schedule playtests at milestones when behavior or level design needs human validation. Which part of your game should be covered by which method right now? Unit Testing vs Integration Testing vs Playtesting means unit tests check isolated logic, integration tests check interactions, and playtesting checks human experience and emergent issues.. In practical terms, what each method finds and where it fits in your workflow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Comparison
keyIdea.text: Unit tests check isolated logic, integration tests check interactions, and playtesting checks human experience and emergent issues.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Testing Types
Unit Tests

Fast and deterministic checks of single methods or classes. Best for pure logic and edge cases.

Example: Verifying PlayerStats.TakeDamage clamps health to zero.
Integration Tests

Validate that systems work together: movement, physics, UI, and combat flows.

Example: Simulate an attack and assert enemy health and damage text display.
Playtesting

Human players reveal UX, balance, and performance concerns that code tests cannot judge.

Example: Players repeatedly miss a jump because camera timing feels off.
When to choose
Unit for logic, integration for interactions, playtesting for experience.
Workflow
Run unit tests frequently, integration tests on PRs, playtests during design checkpoints.
Key Takeaway
Use all three methods to cover technical correctness and player experience.

screens.title: Bug Reporting and Regression Testing
screens.subtitle: Turn a discovered issue into a regression-proof fix

narration.text: When a bug is discovered, either in automated tests or during playtesting, follow a structured reporting process: reproduce, document, isolate, fix, and regress. A good bug report includes steps to reproduce, expected and actual behavior, environment details, and any relevant logs or screenshots. After reproducing the issue, write a failing automated test that captures the bug if possible; this test becomes the regression test. Then implement a minimal fix and run the full test suite to ensure nothing else breaks. Regression testing prevents the same bug from returning in future changes. Avoid vague reports like "it broke"; instead provide precise reproduction steps so developers can recreate the context. For playtest findings that are design-related, include session recordings, player quotes, and a suggested acceptance criteria. A frequent pitfall is fixing a symptom without adding a regression test; that leaves the project vulnerable to reintroducing the bug. By converting discovered bugs into automated checks when feasible, you build a growing safety net. Which recent bug in your project would be useful to capture as a regression test? Bug Reporting and Regression Testing means reproduce the bug, write a failing test when possible, fix it, and run regression tests to ensure the issue stays resolved.. In practical terms, turn a discovered issue into a regression-proof fix. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Regression flow
keyIdea.text: Reproduce the bug, write a failing test when possible, fix it, and run regression tests to ensure the issue stays resolved.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Bug & Regression
Bug report essentials
  • Steps to reproduce with precise input and state.
  • Expected vs actual behavior.
  • Environment details: platform, editor version, and scene if relevant.
  • Attach logs or screenshots if available.
Regression workflow
  1. Reproduce and write a failing test when possible.
  2. Implement minimal fix.
  3. Run full test suite and verify green.
  4. Close the bug with the regression test in place.
Tip
Automate running regression tests in CI so fixes remain verified across branches.
Common mistake
Fixing without a regression test leaves the bug likely to return after refactors.
Key Takeaway
Turn bugs into tests whenever possible to prevent future regressions and speed debugging.

screens.title: Playtesting: Structured Human Feedback
screens.subtitle: Designing playtests that reveal UX and design issues

narration.text: Playtesting is the human side of QA: it uncovers clarity, balance, and enjoyment concerns that automated tests cannot. Effective playtesting begins with clear objectives—what do you want to learn? Choose participants who represent the target audience and give them tasks with observable success criteria. Use structured feedback forms to capture both quantitative and qualitative data, record sessions when possible, and observe behavior rather than only relying on verbal reports. For example, if you want to test a crafting UI, ask players to craft a specific item and note time to completion, errors made, and their comments. A common mistake is to run unstructured playtests that produce vague feedback; structure helps you turn observations into actionable changes. After tests, prioritize discovered issues by severity and frequency, then write clear bug reports or feature tickets. Remember to follow up after fixes with quick regression playtests to confirm the changes improved the experience. Playtesting complements automated tests and helps you build games players enjoy. What specific question would you ask a player in your next playtest? Playtesting: Structured Human Feedback means set objectives, use tasks and measurements, observe behavior, and convert findings into prioritized fixes.. In practical terms, designing playtests that reveal ux and design issues. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Playtest design
keyIdea.text: Set objectives, use tasks and measurements, observe behavior, and convert findings into prioritized fixes.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Playtesting
Design a session
  1. Define objective and tasks.
  2. Pick representative players and environment.
  3. Observe, record, and collect structured feedback.
Measurement
Use time-on-task, error counts, and Likert-style responses combined with open comments to capture both behavior and sentiment.
Example task

Follow-up
Turn validated issues into prioritized tickets and schedule regression playtests after fixes.
Key Takeaway
Structured playtests reveal user-facing problems that automated tests cannot and guide meaningful design fixes.

screens.title: Hands-on: Unit Testing an Inventory Class
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step Edit Mode test assembly and common tests to write

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks you through building an Inventory class and a set of Edit Mode tests that exercise its behavior. Implement an Inventory with an internal dictionary mapping item names to quantities, and expose methods to AddItem, RemoveItem, HasItem, and GetItemQuantity. In tests, create a fresh Inventory instance in a setup method, then write tests for adding a new item, increasing quantity for an existing item, removing items correctly, and handling edge cases like zero or negative amounts. A recommended test checks that removing more items than available returns false and does not change quantity. Another test ensures AddItem ignores invalid names and non-positive quantities. Place these tests in an Edit Mode test assembly so they run quickly. Run them in the Unity Test Runner and confirm green results. If a test fails, read the assert message and adjust the Inventory implementation or the test expectation. This activity teaches practical test writing, determinism, and how to convert bugs into regression tests. Which Inventory method would you test first and why? screens.title: Integrating Tests into Your Development Cycle
screens.subtitle: Where tests fit: local dev, pull requests, and CI

narration.text: Tests are most effective when integrated into everyday workflows. Locally, run fast Edit Mode tests frequently while you develop to catch regressions early. Add integration or focused Play Mode tests to pull requests when changes touch runtime behavior—these should be targeted so PR checks remain fast. In continuous integration, run the full test suite including longer Play Mode checks on scheduled builds or on merge to main, keeping the quick feedback loop responsive for developers. Use test assemblies to separate Edit Mode and Play Mode tests and configure CI to run these appropriately. When a regression appears, triage quickly using failing test context and link failures to bug reports. Automating tests on CI also helps enforce quality gates; require passing critical test groups before merging critical systems. A common trap is letting test suites become slow and brittle; prevent that by pruning overly broad tests, using focused assertions, and grouping slow tests to run less frequently. The goal is a feedback system that is fast for developers and comprehensive for releases. Which part of your pipeline could accept one more quick automated test today?

keyIdea.title: Integration timeline
keyIdea.text: Run fast tests locally, targeted integration tests on PRs, and full suites in CI to balance speed and coverage.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Dev Cycle
Test placement timeline
Local dev
Run Edit Mode tests while coding. Fast feedback prevents regressions.
Pull requests
Run targeted integration or Play Mode tests relevant to changes before merging.
CI / Release
Run full suites including slower Play Mode checks on scheduled or merge builds for release confidence.
Pitfall
Allowing test suites to become slow reduces developer test frequency and undermines coverage.
Key Takeaway
Balance speed and coverage by placing tests at the right stage in your pipeline.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Quick reminders you should keep in mind

narration.text: Keep these core concepts in mind as you work: first, QA is a layered practice—use unit tests for isolated logic, integration and Play Mode tests for system interactions, and playtesting for player-facing experience. Second, the Unity Test Runner supports Edit Mode and Play Mode contexts; choose the one that matches whether your test needs the runtime. Third, write focused, independent tests that follow arrange, act, assert and guard edge cases; convert discovered bugs into regression tests. These practices make development safer and allow you to iterate confidently. Remember that automated tests and human playtests serve different purposes and are both required for a polished game. Use CI to run tests at appropriate stages, keep slow tests grouped and run less frequently, and keep failing test messages clear so fixes are rapid. Which of these three concepts will you apply first in your next development task?

keyIdea.text: Layer tests, choose the right Unity test context, and convert bugs into regression checks for robust QA.

Finally, adopt a workflow where bugs discovered either during automated runs or playtests are turned into regression tests when practical. This practice ensures fixes remain fixed and your team gains confidence when refactoring. These steps together create a reliable, maintainable quality assurance process that protects both code and player experience. Which of these three will you add to your next sprint?
